## Question
What is the correct mathematical construction for priors? That is, what mathematics capture the essence of what a prior is empirically? 

Do priors require symmetric monoidal structure, cartesian structure, multi-sorted cartesian structure, or a more general doctrine depending on the kind of prior? Partly why logical priors and geometric priors give rise to the same notion of a "prior" in Nye's work is that finitary monads on $\mathbf{Set}$ are equivalent to Lawvere theories. What about non-finitary priors? Are there any examples of such priors? 

## Answers log

- **2026-08-27:** Both logical and geometric priors are essentially formalized using the construction of finitary monads. The relationship I see here is that a group action monad is a finitary monad on $\mathbf{Set}$, a Lawvere theory that encodes logical priors is isomorphic to a finitary monad on $\mathbf{Set}$. So my best answer right now is to look further into $\mathbf{Prior}$ as $\mathbf{Mnd}_{f,\mathbf{Set}}$.

## Exploration
The general pattern across many forms of priors is that it consists a specification, a way to transform the specification to input data, and a separate way to transform it to output data. This is described functorially, where one maps abstract data types in the specification to concrete data spaces in a base category. Then, a model (technically, a morphism in some relevant base category), *respects the prior* if it is composed out of components that form a natural transformation between the specification transformations.

### Priors as monads
A prior specification can be regarded as a monad $M$, with prior representations as monad algebras $(X,\alpha_{X})$ and $(Y,\alpha_{Y})$. Then, a model $f\in{}\mathcal{C}(X,Y)$ respects the prior if it can be viewed as a monad algebra homomorphism $(X,\alpha_{X})\xrightarrow{f}(Y,\alpha_{Y})$.

This is studied in [[../../../literature/gavranovic-2024-position-categorical|gavranovic-2024-position-categorical]], where the key example is of group equivariance being recovered by specifying a group action monad. Let $\mathcal{C}=\mathbf{Vect}$, and $M=(G\times-,\eta,\mu)$ be the group action monad on $\mathbf{Set}$. Consider two algebras $(X,\alpha_{X})$ and $(Y,\alpha_{Y})$, defined by structure maps $G\times X\to{}X$, $x\mapsto g\cdot x$, and likewise for $\alpha_{Y}$. Then, a morphism of algebras $(X,\alpha_{X})\to{}(Y,\alpha_{Y})$ is, by definition, a morphism $f:X\to{}Y$ of $\mathcal{C}$ such that the following diagram commutes:
$$f\circ{}\alpha_{X}=\alpha_{Y}\circ{}G\times f.$$
This unpacks to the usual equivariance constraint:
$$f(g\cdot x)=g\cdot f(x).$$


### Priors as Lawvere theories
A prior specification can be regarded as a Lawvere theory $\mathbb{L}$, with prior representations as models (i.e., product-preserving functors) $X,Y:\mathbb{L}\to{}\mathcal{C}$. Then, a model $f$ respects the prior if it can be viewed as a natural transformation $f:X\Rightarrow{}Y$.

One can construct and generalize group equivariance using this approach as well. Define $\mathbb{L}_{G}$ to be the group Lawvere theory, generated freely by an algebraic theory $(\Sigma,\Phi)$ and quotiented out by the equational laws in $\Phi$. In this case:
$$\begin{align}
\Sigma & =\{ s_{g}:1\to{}1 \mid{}\forall{}g\in{}G \}, \\
\Phi & =\{ s_{gh}=s_{g}\circ{}s_{h} \ \forall{}g,h\in{}G,\ s_{e}=\text{id}_{1} \}.
\end{align}$$
Then:
$$\mathbb{L}_{G}=F_{\times}(\Sigma)/\sim_{\Phi},$$
where $F_{\times}(\Sigma)$ is the free category with finite products generated by the operations in $\Sigma$, before imposing (via quotienting) the axioms (i.e., equational laws) in $\Phi$. Now, group actions can be constructed via models of $\mathbb{L}_{G}$. In particular, define:
$$\begin{align}
X(1) & =a, & X(s_{g}) & =\cdot_{X}\ , \\
Y(1) & =b, & Y(s_{g}) & =\cdot_{Y}\ .
\end{align}$$
Then, a natural transformation $f:X\Rightarrow{}Y$ is a collection:
$$f=\{ f_{1}:X(1)\to{}Y(1) \}$$
such that naturality holds:
$$\cdot_{b}\circ{}f_{1}=f_{1}\circ{}\cdot_{a}$$
which, element-wise, leads to the same equivariance constraint:
$$f(g\cdot x)=g\cdot f(x).$$

There are some nuances here. First, $f=f_{1}$ in the above example, since in a Lawvere theory, all objects are generated by $1$:
$$n=\prod_{i=1}^{n}1.$$
Second, Lawvere theories are equivalent to finitary monads on $\mathbf{Set}$:
$$\mathbf{Law}\cong{}\mathbf{Mnd}_{f,\mathbf{Set}}.$$
Lawvere theories cannot describe non-finitary prior specifications, but it can describe logical priors more natively than monads can. For example, in [[../../../literature/nye-2025-categorical-construction|nye-2025-categorical-construction]], one can consider a boolean prior:
$$\begin{align}
\Sigma & =\{ \land:2\to{}1,\ \lor:2\to{}1,\ \lnot:1\to{}1 \}, \\
\Phi & =\{ \lnot\circ{}\land=\lor \circ{}(\lnot \times\lnot) \}.
\end{align}$$
### Priors as PROPs
It is important to establish the relations between monads and PROPs, as they are fundamentally different ways to encode algebraic theories. First, PROPs are a generalization of Lawvere theories. The general symmetric monoidal structure of a PROP allows it to encode multi-output operations, whereas in Lawvere theories, such operation collapses to $f : m → 1$ by the universal property of the (cartesian) product. Since we want access to these multi-output operations (e.g., attention mechanisms), we favor PROPs over Lawvere theories. This also allows us to model complex tasks where the neural network might output many metrics (e.g. detecting objects and predicting their coordinates). 

Nonetheless, a prior specification is a PROP, representations are models, and a admissible model is a monoidal natural transformation. Interestingly, we can see that the space of natural transformations is isomorphic to monoidal natural transformations in the case in [[../constructions/priors-as-triples-of-specification-representations|priors-as-triples-of-specification-representations]]. 

We can also use colored PROPs to describe even more general syntax.
